name: Catedral de Santa Eulàlia
blurb: Started in the 13th century, left with a bare front wall around 1460. The ornate facade you see today was added between 1887 and 1913, paid for by a banker and based on a 1408 drawing. Thirteen geese live in the cloister, one for each year of Saint Eulàlia's life.

name: Santa Maria del Mar
blurb: Built in 55 years (1329-1383), which is nothing by cathedral standards. One uninterrupted space, octagonal columns thirteen metres apart. The stones were carried down Montjuïc by port workers, the bastaixos, whose portraits are carved into the main portal.

name: Catedral de Santa Maria
blurb: Begun around 1171 in solid Romanesque, finished in Gothic. Round arches below, pointed arches above. It stands on the highest point of Roman Tarraco, where the Temple of Augustus once stood, confirmed by excavations under the nave in 2010.
tag: A change of mind carved in stone

name: Monestir de Santa Maria
blurb: Founded in 879 by Wilfred the Hairy, count of Barcelona, who is buried inside. The 12th-century portal is a full wall of sculpted stone, a Bible in stone for people who could not read. A mob burned the monastery in 1835; the portal survived, the monks never came back.

name: Basilique Saint-Nazaire
blurb: Hidden inside the fortress most visitors never find. A dark 11th-century Romanesque nave in front, a light-flooded Gothic choir behind. Simon de Montfort, the crusade's feared commander, was buried here in 1218 after a siege engine crushed his skull.

name: Cathédrale Saint-André
blurb: Eleanor of Aquitaine married the future Louis VII here in 1137, a marriage that failed and triggered three centuries of Anglo-French war. The bell tower stands twenty metres apart from the church, built on its own foundations so the bells would not shake the walls loose.
tag: Where three centuries of war began

name: Cathédrale Saint-Front
blurb: Five domes on a Greek cross plan, closer to Saint Mark's in Venice than to anything else in France. Restorer Paul Abadie rebuilt the domes in the 19th century, then used Saint-Front as the model for his next commission: the Sacré-Coeur in Paris.
tag: The original before the Sacré-Coeur copy

name: Abbaye de Cadouin
blurb: Austere Cistercian Romanesque church next to a flamboyant Gothic cloister. For eight centuries the abbey lived off a relic said to be Christ's burial cloth. In 1934 scholars read the woven text: Arabic, praising an 11th-century Fatimid caliph. The pilgrimage stopped overnight.
tag: The relic that read as a forgery

name: Église Saint-Étienne
blurb: Consecrated in 1097 as a Cluniac priory church, almost exactly as the 11th century left it. Among the earliest surviving churches to combine a stone barrel vault with three storeys and direct window light, the structural puzzle Gothic architecture would later solve at scale.
tag: Where Gothic's problem was first posed

name: Collégiale Saint-Thiébaut
blurb: A regional saying ranks the towers: Strasbourg's is tallest, Freiburg's broadest, Thann's the most beautiful. The spire, finished in 1516, is 78 metres of openwork stone carved thin enough to see sky through. The west portal carries some 500 sculpted figures.

name: Sainte-Chapelle (Château des ducs de Savoie)
blurb: Home to the Shroud of Turin from 1502 to 1578, when it was still the Shroud of Chambéry. A fire on the night of 4 December 1532 melted the silver reliquary; the burn marks on the shroud date from that night, not from Jerusalem. The relic left for Turin in 1578.

name: Saint-Pierre de Montmartre
blurb: Thirty metres from the Sacré-Coeur, consecrated in 1147 by Pope Eugene III with Bernard of Clairvaux at his side. One of the oldest churches in Paris. The riders pass it three times in one afternoon, at roughly forty kilometres per hour, on the final circuit up Montmartre.
